# The problem

## What modelling evidence has to be

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
- Chris Whitty, then Chief Scientific Adviser at the Department for
  International Development and later Chief Medical Officer for
  England, set out what evidence has to be to inform policy
- Timely enough to still be useful, explicit about its methods, and as
  simple as it can be while staying rigorous
- Add collaborative, because no one group holds all the data or all the
  expertise
- Almost nothing we build is all of these at once

::: {.callout-important}
The trade-off is not between good and bad models. It is between
rigour and being able to move.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}

## Joint models work, and they do not transfer

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
- England's COVID-19 models fitted cases, prevalence, severity, and bed
  occupancy together, and that evidence reached policy
- Each took expertise across several domains, and a long time
- In 2022 mpox spread through sexual contact networks. Those models
  could not represent that
- New single-source models were built instead, at speed
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
![](../figures/composable-birrell.png){width="100%"

::: {.attribution}

## Chaining models loses information

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
- The ONS COVID-19 Infection Survey tested over four million swabs from
  more than 150,000 households at a cost above £500 million. Modellers
  outside saw the published prevalence, not the swabs
- Prevalence fed incidence and $R_t$, and those fed variant
  transmissibility and severity
- Uncertainty was approximated at each step and assumptions were
  inherited unchecked
- We rebuilt a chain like this for a different problem and found bias
  at every stage. Fitting the steps together removed it

::: {.callout-important}
Joint fitting is the fix, and it hands you a model nobody can take
apart.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
![](../figures/composable-ons-cascade.jpg){width="94%"
fig-align="center"}

::: {.attribution}
The chain fitted as one model instead. Prevalence (A), incidence (B),
antibody prevalence (C) and $R_t$ (D) estimated together from the
survey data. Abbott and Funk (2022),
[doi:10.1101/2022.03.29.22273101](https://doi.org/10.1101/2022.03.29.22273101).
Survey figures from the paper's introduction
:::
:::
::::

## So everyone rebuilds the whole model

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
- At least seven packages estimate $R_t$ by renewal in Stan. Only two
  of them share any component, and I wrote both
- The wastewater $R_t$ tools make different choices about how much of
  the sampling to represent, and share nothing. It is not clear which
  of those choices matter
- Shared parts do exist. `primarycensored` is one, and uptake outside
  my own packages is thin
- In multi-model work, shared parts would let you attribute a
  difference in results to an assumption rather than to an
  implementation

::: {.callout-important}
The unit of reuse is the whole model, not the epidemiology inside it.
:::
